subject: advantages of irt modeling in stan compared to em algorithm

messages.author: 71bfb5f1e96782a8
messages.subject: advantages of irt modeling in stan compared to em algorithm
parts:
Dear stan-users,

the reason I started to use stan for irt modeling was that I wanted to include prior information about the item parameters in the estimation of a graded response model. it took some time but finally, i was able to conduct the analysis as I had imagined. however, I now learned that it's also possible to use prior information in the em-algorithm as employed in the r-package mirt and this leads to almost the same results (stan gives me the mean of the posterior and mirt gives me the mode, but item parameters, ability estimates almost the same), but mcmc is considerably slower (hrs against seconds).

can you give me some reasons, why/when i should use mcmc-sampling? my thoughts are:
- it seems more straightforward for me to employ something like a latent regression in stan
- posterior predictive checks are easy to do in stan and interpretation is straightforward, but could be done also, when model parameters come from the em-algorithm
- hierarchical irt models?

would be great if you could give me some insights, thanks for taking your time, felix

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advantages of irt modeling in stan compared to em algorithm
parts:
That's a huge question! EM gives you a penalized maximum likelihood
estimate (MLE), whereas MCMC gives you a Bayesian posterior. The
basics of these are described in the Stan manual part on inference.

You should read a textbook on Bayes.

The main motivations for Bayes is that the modeling is more flexible, the
estimation is more reliable (MLE has lots of pathologies, including
not existing in hierarchical models without zero-avoiding priors), and
you get a characterization of your posterior uncertainty not only in
parameter estimates, but also in predcitions.

If you really meant EM, you have to code EM on a case-by-case basis.
But you could skip EM and just use Stan's optimizer if all you want is
a fast penalized MLE. It'll probably be faster than a custom EM
implementation.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advantages of irt modeling in stan compared to em algorithm
parts:
The big difference is that MCMC will quantify the _entire posterior distribution_
and not just a single expectation.  Importantly, IRT models have complex
uncertainties that EM cannot quantify and you really should care about those
uncertainties in practice.  

I’m going to guess that you wrote your IRT model using a centered 
parameterization — it should be much faster with anon-centered parameterization.
But in any case we really can’t comment on raw timings without seeing the code.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advantages of irt modeling in stan compared to em algorithm
parts:
> On Jan 25, 2017, at 4:44 PM, Dr. Hans Hansen <drhans...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ah, i think you mean: You should read a textbook on Bayes again. :P
>
> btw, i don't really want to implement em by myself... but r-package mirt uses em and does something bayesian, when one specifies priors: it combines the prespecified prior with the ml estimate to get the mode of the posterior.

So does Stan. That's just "penalized maximum likelihood estimation"
where the penalty is expressed as a prior. So while you can look
at it as a Bayesian model, finding a mode is *not* Bayesian inference.
> so, it seems like another way of obtaining the posterior.

No! It finds a posterior mode. The posterior is a *distribution*.
Not all models even have posterior modes, such as mixture models or
hierarchical models with the usual priors.
> i wonder when this is the way to go and when mcmc-sampling in stan is more reasonable.

MCMC sampling in Stan gives you draws from the posterior, letting
you do Bayesian inference. It's always better if you can afford
the compute time, assuming whoever you need to work with (bosses,
colleagues, editors, grant managers, etc.) will let you apply
Bayesian methods.

- Bob
